title: Quantum Optimal Control Primer
abstract: This is a set of detailed notes that are part of a Ph.D. Course on Quantum Control delivered at the Department of Chemistry of Seoul National University in 2014. Part of this course was also taught in the Department of Chemistry of the Friedrich Schiller University Jena. It focuses on quantum optimal control and quantum optimal control algorithms based on the gradient and extended gradient methods.
summary: This paper serves as a detailed theoretical primer on Quantum Optimal Control (QOC), outlining the mathematical framework for steering quantum systems to target states using external fields. It rigorously derives the necessary conditions for optimality and systematically compares several advanced, convergent numerical algorithms (like Krotov and fast-kick-off) required to solve the resulting complex, nonlinear equations.
main_problem: The core problem is finding the time-dependent external field $\epsilon(t)$ that drives an initial quantum state $|\psi(0)angle$ to a desired target state $|\phi_tangle$ with maximum probability.
main_result: The optimal control field $\epsilon_{oc}(t)$ is determined by solving the variational condition $\delta J / \delta \epsilon(t) = 0$, leading to complex, nonlinear equations requiring iterative solvers.
method: The paper develops and compares several iterative algorithms, including gradient methods, Krotov-type schemes, and fast-kick-off algorithms, all rooted in variational calculus.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as an isolated molecule whose dynamics are governed by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE) with a Hamiltonian $\hat{H}(t) = \hat{H}_0 - \mu\epsilon(t)$. The control is applied via an external classical field $\epsilon(t)$ acting through the dipole interaction.
key_observables: The objective function $J = \langle\psi(T)|\hat{P}|\psi(T)angle$ (transition probability), and the time evolution of observables $\langle \psi(t)|\hat{A}|\psi(t)angle$.
important_parameters: The control field parameters (frequencies, intensities, phases) and the convergence parameters for the iterative schemes ($\gamma, \eta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the dipole approximation and assumes the external field $\epsilon(t)$ can be treated classically. The derivation of algorithms often involves first-order variations.
paper_structure: The structure moves from defining the general problem (QC) to deriving the variational condition for optimality, and finally comparing and detailing multiple advanced numerical algorithms (Gradient, Krotov, Fast-kick-off) to solve the resulting implicit equations.
why_interesting: This work provides a comprehensive, advanced theoretical toolkit for manipulating quantum systems using external fields, which is central to quantum optics and molecular control studies.
